function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

I’m not able to actually clone repositories, run commands on your machine, or push commits back to GitHub.  
What I can do is walk you through the exact steps you’d need to take locally (or in a CI environment) and give you ready‑to‑copy templates for the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow that you can drop into the repository.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# SSH clone – make sure you have the proper key set up
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you prefer HTTPS or don’t have SSH keys set up, replace the URL with  
> `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git` and authenticate with your GitHub credentials.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repository & generate artefacts

Below is a quick‑look at the repo structure (you can confirm this by running `tree -a` or `ls -R`):

```
nodejs-welcome/
├─ .github/
│  └─ workflows/
├─ src/
│  ├─ index.js
│  └─ ...
├─ package.json
├─ README.md
└─ ...
```

### 2.1 Create / update the Dockerfile

Because the repo is a Node.js application, a minimal Dockerfile looks like this:

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder

WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Build the app (if you have a build step)
# RUN npm run build

# Runtime stage
FROM node:20-alpine AS runtime

WORKDIR /app

# Copy only the built artifacts + node_modules
COPY --from=builder /app/package*.json ./
COPY --from=builder /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist   # adjust if you build to dist
COPY --from=builder /app/src ./src     # fallback if no dist

EXPOSE 3000

CMD ["node", "src/index.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * Uses multi‑stage builds to keep the final image small.  
> * Installs only production dependencies (`npm ci --omit=dev`).  
> * Exposes port `3000` – the default port used by many Node.js apps (adjust if your app listens elsewhere).  

If you already have a Dockerfile in the repo, replace its contents with the snippet above or merge the changes.

### 2.2 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a new directory for the manifests (if it doesn’t exist):

```bash
mkdir -p k8s
```

#### Deployment (`k8s/deployment.yaml`)

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # adjust registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
        resources:
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "512Mi"
          requests:
            cpu: "250m"
            memory: "256Mi"
```

#### Service (`k8s/service.yaml`)

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Notes**  
> * The `image` field should point to the image you’ll push to a registry (GitHub Container Registry, Docker Hub, etc.).  
> * Adjust `replicas`, resource limits, and environment variables to match your production needs.

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a new workflow file:

```bash
mkdir -p .github/workflows
touch .github/workflows/build-and-push.yml
```

#### `.github/workflows/build-and-push.yml`

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write   # needed for GHCR

    steps:
    - name: Checkout repository
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Cache node modules
      uses: actions/cache@v4
      with:
        path: ~/.npm
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-node-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-node-

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: |
          ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
          ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
```

> **Why this workflow?**  
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Builds the image using Docker Buildx (supports multi‑platform builds).  
> * Pushes two tags: `latest` and the commit SHA.  
> * Uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` for authentication – no extra secrets required.  

---

## 3️⃣ Add all changed files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/build-and-push.yml
```

> If you modified an existing Dockerfile, just `git add Dockerfile` again.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> **Tip** – If you’re on a different branch or want to force push, adjust the command accordingly.

---

### Quick sanity check

After pushing, you should see:

* A new **Actions** tab with a successful run for “Build & Push Docker Image”.  
* The image pushed to `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome`.  
* The `k8s` directory containing `deployment.yaml` and `service.yaml`.  
* The updated `Dockerfile` at the repo root.

You can now apply the Kubernetes manifests to your cluster:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/
```

---

## Recap

| Step | Command / Action |
|------|------------------|
| 1 | `git clone ... && cd nodejs-welcome` |
| 2.1 | Create Dockerfile (see snippet) |
| 2.2 | Create `k8s/deployment.yaml` & `k8s/service.yaml` |
| 2.3 | Create `.github/workflows/build-and-push.yml` |
| 3 | `git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/build-and-push.yml` |
| 4 | `git commit -m "..." && git push origin main` |

Feel free to tweak the resource limits, environment variables, or image registry to match your own infrastructure. Let me know if you hit any snags or need help customizing any part!
